# Glossary

## Concepts

**Cognitive offloading.** Hand off the _how_. Keep the _why_ and the _what_. The human still has a view of the change to compare against.

**Cognitive surrender.** Stop constructing an answer and adopt the tool's answer, with no _why_ or _what_ of your own. That is how comprehension debt grows.

**Comprehension debt.** The gap between the code in the system and the understanding the humans who develop, maintain, or operate it have. Unlike technical debt, nobody chooses it. It stays invisible until something breaks.

**The title.** Short name for the whole change. Always written. Prefer a user-created title (pull request, ticket, transcript) when it names this change. Invent one when that title is missing, vague, or names something else.

**The why.** Why this work exists. The skill writes it from tickets, issues, PR comments, coding-agent transcripts and any existing human or agent generated that's related to the change. One for the whole change when those sources name one story. Omit it when they are silent or mixed. One on every group. A group with no source of its own may exist to enable later groups. Do not invent a motive from the patch.

**The what.** What this change is. Always written. Document `summary` is the whole change. Group `summary` is that group. Named so a human has a view before they read the diff.

**The how.** How the change is implemented. The live git diff is the how. The agent may group and summarize it. The agent must not replace it.

**Attention.** The one judgment call a reviewer makes in a group: what the code at head does, where it matters, and the decision. At most one per group, and most groups have none. `kind` is `contract`, `tradeoff`, `product`, or `risk`. A bug, a missing test, a nit, a refactor idea, or anything settled in review is not an attention. Other tools hunt bugs; an attention points at the call only the maintainer can make.

**Questions.** At most 2 per group. Each asks why the change is this way, where the code and the sources leave the reason open. When a source answers it, the answer goes in the why. The UI copies each question into a prompt for the agent that wrote the change.

**Focus range.** Lines of one hunk the UI opens first, labeled Agent focus, with a caption that says why to read them: on one side, inside one live hunk of the group, at most 25 lines. An added file gets none. A row at each cut edge counts the lines not shown, and one click shows the whole hunk. `validate` fails a range that leaves its hunk.

**Note.** One or two sentences pinned to one line of a hunk the group covers. It says what the code alone does not say. At most three per group, lettered A, B, C in the UI. A judgment call is an attention, not a note.

**File note.** One line on one file of a group: what changed in that file, past what the group summary says. Keyed by the file's head path. A generated or mechanical file gets a short one. `validate` fails a note on a path the group does not cover.

**Look for.** Document-level source verdicts: each source item done differently, not done, or not true at head, each manual step a source says the change needs, and each instruction a source gives a reviewer. Cite the source. Do not store a pass/fail. The skill writes the comparison; the field is only the place for it.

**Source.** A ticket, pull request, PR comment, commit, or transcript the skill read to write its prose. Locators plus a gist. PR comments also copy author, body, and an optional line pin. The pin is the line that comment still sits on at head, on an open thread. A resolved thread and an outdated comment keep the source and omit the pin. Transcripts have no URL.

**Citation.** A markdown link `[text](source:id)` in the why, the what, an attention, a question, a focus caption, a note, a file note, or lookFor. The UI turns it into a mark. `validate` fails on an unknown id.

## Code

**Review document.** Interpretation only. Title, groups, summaries, optional generated why, optional attentions, questions, focus ranges, notes, and file notes, optional lookFor, sources, hunk pointers. Never patch text. Source refs must resolve in cwd.

**Group.** Schema `groups` item. The UI uses the same word.

**Review concern.** Why these hunks are read together. Not a directory, unless that directory is the concern.

**Part / story.** Independent work. Could have been its own PR. `dependsOn` only inside a story.

**Size.** Review burden. Not file or hunk count.

**Hunk ref.** Pointer into live git. Copy from the `review` skeleton. Never invent.

**Index.** Internal hunk list. No line content. Not stored in the UI. `review` writes those refs into a covering skeleton.

**Live git.** `git` in cwd at serve time. Git wins.

**Coverage.** Every live hunk in at least one group. Duplicates allowed.

**Unassigned.** Live hunks with no group. Still shown.

**Stale ref.** Pointer that does not match live git. Serve still starts. Do not invent a replacement.

**Refresh.** Carry a review over to new commits. A hunk with the same path and the same added and removed lines is the same hunk; its ref follows it. Focus ranges and notes follow a same hunk and drop with a changed or gone one. A file note stays while every hunk of its file is same. A hunk edited in the same region of the file is changed and keeps its group; its prose is re-checked. Any other hunk is new or gone. `source.baseSha` and `source.headSha` record where the last review stood. The last review stays beside the new one, named in `previous`; the UI's What changed page compares the two.

**Skill.** Grouping instructions. Does not talk to git.

**CLI.** review, pregroup, digest, show, refresh, validate, serve, export. Cwd is the repo. `review` and `pregroup` write a covering draft only; the skill fills interpretation.
